variants.intertext: The second chapter of the Standard Babylonian @i{Atraḫasīs} is known from one Sippar manuscript (SipNB1), two from Babylon (BabNB1 and BabNB2), and two to four from Nineveh (NinNA1-NinNA4). While the text across manuscripts is similar, chapter divisions differ. This edition reconstructs the ‘Sippar Library’ version, whose manuscript has been restored in 2024 and collated for this edition. The ‘Sippar Library’ manuscript of chapter II runs parallel to OB @i{Atramḫasīs} I 103–230.

manuscripts.atf:
k[a-ak]-ki#-ka li-i-qe₂ ṣi-i ap-pu-uh₂#-ri#
#note: See @bib{RN118@185}: “The plene writing of the first vowel in @akk{li-i-qe₂} (II 8) is unwanted, but reveals that for one LB scribe, at least, the I/1 imperative of @i{leqû} followed the pattern of @i{limad} and @i{rikab} (also @i{pišah}, @i{tikal}, @i{tišab}, etc.) rather than @i{mahaṣ}. Among verbs III-weak (@i{e}), of course, the pattern followed by the imperative in Babylonian is usually uncertain because of the ambiguities of script: e.g. @i{pete} or @i{pite}, @i{šeme} or @i{šime}, @i{ṭehe} or @i{ṭihe}? (cf. @bib{RN27201@§105 f}). Verbs III-weak (@i{a}) with attested I/1 imperatives are rare, but @i{kila} is standard and @i{tima} (Bab.) is found alongside @i{tama} (Ass.); note also OA @i{kita} < @i{katā'um}. On this evidence, slim though it is, the pattern @i{limad} appears to be typical of such verbs, and presumably ought to be of verbs III-weak (@i{e}) also. Accordingly the spelling @akk{li-i-qe₂} might be taken as orthographic evidence for an imperative @i{liqe} in preference to @i{leqe}, though obviously it would be foolish to insist that a variant @i{leqe} never occurred.”

variants.reconstruction:
%n ibbalkitū | hupšu | issi
#note: See @bib{RN118@185}: “In the synonym list Explicit @i{Malku} II [N.B. now edited by @bib{RN500@290–291}] the word @i{hupšu} is equated with @i{nišu} (@bib{temp_id_2401129561684543 442@j}), and in a commentary on @i{Šumma ālu}, with @i{ṣābū}(@akk{ERIN₂-MEŠ}) [x] (@bib{UBHD-LS@140} @url{/fragmentarium/K.4229}{K.4229}, 12). These equivalences indicate only that @i{hupšu} refers to a group of people. In the army the @i{hupšu} is indeed the mass of common soldiers, but more relevant to our passage is its use to denote a labour gang engaged in public works, as in the omen apodosis @i{tīb} @akk{hup₂-ši mar-ri u tup-ši-[ik-ki]}, “mutiny of spade-gang and basket-gang” (@bib{RN2605@442, rev. 2}), and in an inscription of Sargon II: @akk{[...] eṭlūti(GURUŠ)-MEŠ-šu₂ il-ku tup-šik-ku mar-ṣi-iš u₂# im-ta-ni ṣāb(ERIN₂)-MEŠ hup-šiš}, “[he imposed on] his male population the grievous burden of corvée-work and basket-carrying, [and] counted them among the labour gang” (@bib{UBHD-1553949@1, 33}). The curious plene writing of the first syllable is also found in the line of Explicit @i{Malku} cited above: @akk{[hu]-u₂-up-šu}.”

%n parṣam | tabal-mi || liqe | [...] ...
#note: At the end, the restoration @akk{q]a₂?-at i?#-[di-ka]} (a phrase that would only be attested here) has been proposed by @bib{RN118@186}: “No OB text survives for these three lines ([OB I 171–3]; 174 // MS G ii′ 1). The main problems are the ends of ll. 58 and 60. In the former @bib{RN435} read @akk{li-qi₂ id-ka}, reconstructed from MSS LM (@bib{CT0046@12 and 11}), but the new tablet suggests that there was a longer phrase. The traces of @akk{[...] x at# x [...]} were copied in Baghdad as follows: [@i{Drawing}]. However, for the moment the recovery of the end of l. 58 remains beyond us. From the context a translation along the lines of “Take (my duties) into your own possession!” would be expected.” Another possibility would be to restore at the end the rare word @i{šibqētu} / @i{šibqātu}, a variant of the more common @i{šibqū}, “plan.” The restoration seems possible epigraphically, but the word @i{šibqātu} is very poorly attested, and it appears to be @i{plurale tantum}, whereas the writing in SipNB1 and NinNA1 require a singular (@i{šibqītu}).

variants.reconstruction:
%n ila | ištēn | šisī-ma || [lū ut]eddušū? | parṣū
#note: In the old excavation photo of SipNB1 the sign before @akk{šu₂} has two clear Winkelhaken before the vertical, which render it incompatible with a reading @akk{DI} (cf. @bib{RN118@186}), but also with the @akk{DU} of MS NinNA1. Cf. @bib{RN118@186}: “In I. 60 the new tablet and collation of MS M reveals that the final word is @i{parṣi}. The line no longer appears explicitly to recommend the death of the strikers’ leader, as previously understood. The slaughter of a god is thus first mentioned specifically in SB II 91, where it is the suggestion of Ea. Here, Enlil’s proposal is less easy to determine, since we are handicapped by the manuscripts' disagreement over the verb. MS M has [@i{l}]@i{iddûšu} (pl., @i{nadû}), with the Anunnaki as a plausible subject, but the new tablet appears to have @i{liddīšu} (sing., @i{nadû}), which does not yield good sense, or @i{liddišū}, “let them renew” (pl., @i{edēšu}), which does. Not enough of MS L survives to know how the verb stood in that source. The Assyrian recension possibly has the imperative of @i{nadû} (MS S ii 7: @akk{i-d[i-šu?]}). In the reading offered by the Sippar tablet, we assume that Enlil’s wish is for the Anunnaki, here the great decision-making gods, to set about establishing a new order in the universe (@i{parṣī uddušu}). This is necessary because he himself has abdicated in favour of Anu. However, the search for the instigator of the conflict that began with Nuska’s mission is not to be given up. But there is a difficulty: because the mutinous gods have unanimously accepted joint responsibility for their strike, no one individual can be identified as prime mover. Accordingly, Enlil proposes that Anu summon “a certain god” (@i{ilam ištēn}), that is, any one of his choosing from among the rebels, into the presence of the divine council, which will, implicitly, decide his fate and in doing so establish a new order. The reading preserved on the Kuyunjik manuscript, @i{liddûšu}, is open to a similar interpretation. The meaning of @i{parṣi nadû} is clear from the myth of Anzû, where the phrase describes the overturning of the natural order that follows Enlil’s involuntary loss of his powers (@url{corpus/L/1/10/OB/II#1}{OB Anzû II 1}: @akk{{d}en-lil₂-lu-tam i-te-ki-im na-du-u₂ pa-ar-ṣu₂}, “he snatched the Enlilship, the divine regulations were cast down”; cf. @url{corpus/L/1/10/SB/I#b%2B78}{SB Anzû I 81}: @akk{{d}en-lil₂-u₂-ta il-te-qe₂ na-du-u₂ [par-ṣu]}). In the present context this is perhaps a possible idiom, literally “let them cast down the divine regulations for him.” The natural order of things will be set aside to allow the punishing of one of the rebels, and thereafter re-established.” See also: @bib{RN630@56}: “Die Lesung @bib{RN435@ 52, 151}: @akk{... l[i-id-du-šu₂ tam-ta} ist obsolet, s.a. @bib{pettinato1970review@78–79}, @bib{moran1970creation@52 Anm. 13}. Der Ausdruck @i{parṣī nadû} in [173] M könnte nach @bib{RN118@186} dieselbe Bedeutung von @i{parṣī uddušu} in Si haben: das Niederlegen einer bestehenden göttlichen Ordnung, die nach der Bestrafung eines Gottes wieder hergestellt wird.” Wilcke (@bib{RN1196@77 with fn. 25}) understands the line (reading @i{nadû}) as “Ruf (den) einen Gott! Sie sollen ihm mein Amt auferlegen!”

Hitherto, the only attestation of this verb in the prefix-conjugation of the I/1 stem was the famous line of the Flood Story, @akk{man-za-zu ul i-pa-aš₂-šim-ma}, “no standing place appeared to it" (SB Gilgameš XI 148 // 151). variants.reconstruction:
%n a[lla] | ellil || iṭbuhūšu | mahrīti
#note: See @bib{RN118@187}: “This line replaces older @i{ina puhrīšunu iṭṭabḫū} (OB I 224 [= 220]). The syntax is again in disarray, with the verb @i{iṭbuḫūšu} intruding into the unity of the possessive construction, @i{Ellil maḫrītim} (if maḫrītim seems unconvincing one may read @i{iṭbuhūšūma aḫrīti}, but since the plural @i{mahrâtu} can mean “former times” there seems to us no reason why the singular should not also carry this meaning; cf. the attested analogous pairs @i{aḫrītu} : @i{aḫrâtu}, @i{arkītu} : @i{arkâtu}, @i{pānītu} : @i{pānâtu}). The phrase “an Enlil of old”, meaning a god who was once a senior figure but who later lost his position, is comparable with “the Enlils who rebelled” (@sux{{d}en.lil₂.la₂{meš}} @akk{ša₂ ik-kir-[u₂]}) and “the seven conquered Enlils” (@sux{7 {d}en.lil₂{meš}} @akk{ki-šit-ti} || @sux{7 dingir.dingir dingir{meš}} (= @akk{{d}il₃-il₃-MEŠ?}) @akk{ki-šit-tu₄}) of mythology, and among these, equated with Anšar, Alla was indeed numbered: see @bib{lambert1980theology@65} (the passages there cited have been recently edited by @bib{RN383@155, 17; 194; 198, rev. 8}). If the syntactical disorder of this line is not simply corrupt, we can only suggest that it is intended to highlight the shocking deed retailed. To our knowledge the most obvious parallel is in @i{Enūma eliš} I 81–2, where the great significance of the event described the birth of Marduk induces the poet to repeat the crucial line with an added adjective violating the unity of the possessive construction: @akk{ina qe₂-reb} @i{apsî}(@sux{abzu}) @akk{ib-ba-ni} [@akk{{d}mar]duk} / @i{ina} @akk{qe₂-reb} @i{elli}(@sux{ku₃}) @i{apsî}(@sux{abzu}) @akk{ib-ba-ni} [@akk{{d}marduk}].”
